newsitem.title: KENYA: Mandela to join peace efforts at Zaire summit.
newsitem.headline: Mandela to join peace efforts at Zaire summit.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela will add South Africa's weight and his personal prestige to the stumbling efforts to control the conflict in Zaire and the "Great Lakes" region when African leaders meet in Kenya on Monday.
After months of staying on the sidelines, Mandela has finally bowed to the pressure on South Africa to take an active role in the crisis.
He will join at least six other presidents or prime ministers at the one-day summit in Nairobi called by Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi.
"The president is definitely going," Mandela's spokesman Parks Mankahlana told Reuters on Saturday.
"He was invited and decided to go because he is concerned about the situation, and reports (on Friday) that it may be getting worse."

Kenya's foreign ministry says the summit's agenda is "the crisis in the Great Lakes region". Tension in the area, roughly grouping Zaire, Rwanda, Burundi and parts of Uganda and Tanzania, erupted into full conflict in mid-October.
Ethnic Tutsis in eastern Zaire called the Banyamulenge launched a well-planned rebellion with dissidents from other ethnic groups, routing Zairean troops.
Two months later the rebels control most of the east of Africa's third-largest country. Their goal is to link up with other opponents and end the 31-year reign of Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko.
The ailing Mobutu's aides say he will return to Zaire this week after four months in Europe for cancer surgery and convalescence.
Kenya has invited Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo to Monday's summit but there is no confirmation he will come.

Zaire boycotted the first such summit, held in Nairobi on November 5, refusing to sit down with Rwanda. Kinshasa accuses Rwanda and Uganda of masterminding the rebellion and says Rwandan troops are occupying the east.
Rwanda denies any direct involvement but foreign journalists and aid workers in eastern Zaire have identified some Rwandan troops among the rebels.

The lack of any dialogue between the protagonists is obstructing peace efforts. Western diplomatic sources said a senior Mobutu envoy, who was due to meet Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni and Rwanda's Vice-President Paul Kagame in Kampala last week, failed to turn up.

African mediation is far from united. A summit in Brazzaville on December 3, which Zaire and Burundi attended but which Rwanda and Uganda boycotted, appeared to be a rival initiative to Kenya's, African diplomats say.

Moi's November summit had no impact on the conflict. In vain, it urged the United Nations Security Council to deploy a "neutral force" in eastern Zaire to help 1.2 million Rwandan and Burundian refugees trapped by the fighting.
At least half that number later walked back to Rwanda which they fled in 1994 at the time of the civil war and genocide.
The rest of the Hutu refugees are scattered over a large area and disputes over logistics, numbers and political agendas prevented deployment of an international force to help them.

The military mission was formally abandoned on Saturday, confirming the world's reluctance to get involved in a deep-rooted crisis which African diplomats fear will continue for many years. A Canadian force formed in November never intervened in eastern Zaire and the U.N. ordered the 350 people in it to return home from their bases in Uganda and Rwanda.
"If Zaire should implode it will totally change the map of the region with consequences for the entire continent," a senior Organisation of African Unity (OAU) official told Reuters.
The rebel leader, Laurent Kabila, has not been invited to Monday's summit, Kenyan Foreign Minister Kalonzo Musyoka told Reuters last week.
"We also do not think that would be useful at this stage," the OAU official said. "A lot of groundwork needs to be done before Kabila can be brought in at this level."
In an interview with Reuters on Thursday Kabila, a veteran revolutionary, announced a unilateral ceasefire to help foreign powers coerce Zaire into accepting negotiations.
Zaire's interior minister, Kamanda wa Kamanda, rejected the offer on Friday.

"We do not recognise this ceasefire. In this war we believe that the other side is the government of Rwanda and those who are supporting Rwanda so we shall do everything in own means to recover our territory," he told Reuters in Kinshasa.
Some leaders attending the summit want the related conflict in Burundi to take centre stage, given their lack of influence over events in Zaire.
But Burundi's military government has not been invited.

At least 150,000 people are feared to have died in ethnic war between Tutsis and Hutus in Burundi since 1993. Regional economic sanctions were imposed on Burundi after last July's coup by Major Pierre Buyoya but they have failed to bring the desired political results and some of the leaders expected in Nairobi want the sanctions eased or lifted, diplomats said.
